hints: Order the 12 tourist height estimates in ascending order: $30, 38, 40, 40, 45, 50, 52, 55, 55, 60, 62, 110$.
Find the median by taking the mean of the 6th and 7th values: $\frac{50 + 52}{2}$.

Find the lower quartile $Q_1$ from the lower half (mean of 3rd and 4th values: $\frac{40 + 40}{2} = 40$) and the upper quartile $Q_3$ from the upper half (mean of 9th and 10th values: $\frac{55 + 60}{2} = 57.5$).
Calculate the interquartile range: $\mathrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 57.5 - 40$.
walkthrough:
Sort the 12 data values in ascending order:
$$30, 38, 40, 40, 45, 50, 52, 55, 55, 60, 62, 110$$

Find the median as the average of the 6th and 7th observations ($n = 12$):
$$\text{Median} = \frac{50 + 52}{2} = 51\text{ metres}$$

Find the quartiles by finding the medians of the lower and upper halves of six values:
$$\text{Lower quartile } (Q_1) = \frac{40 + 40}{2} = 40\text{ metres}$$
$$\text{Upper quartile } (Q_3) = \frac{55 + 60}{2} = 57.5\text{ metres}$$

Calculate the interquartile range:
$$\mathrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 57.5 - 40 = 17.5\text{ metres}$$
teacher_walkthrough: We are given $n = 12$ tourist estimates of a building height. We first find the median and interquartile range.

Step 1: Write down the 12 values in ascending order:
$$30, 38, 40, 40, 45, 50, 52, 55, 55, 60, 62, 110$$

Step 2: Find the median ($Q_2$):
Because $n = 12$ is even, the median lies halfway between the 6th and 7th values:
- 6th value $= 50$
- 7th value $= 52$
$$\text{Median} = \frac{50 + 52}{2} = 51\text{ metres}$$

Step 3: Find the lower quartile ($Q_1$):
The lower half consists of the first 6 values: $30, 38, 40, 40, 45, 50$.
The median of these 6 values is the average of the 3rd and 4th values:
$$Q_1 = \frac{40 + 40}{2} = 40\text{ metres}$$

Step 4: Find the upper quartile ($Q_3$):
The upper half consists of the last 6 values: $52, 55, 55, 60, 62, 110$.
The median of these 6 values is the average of the 9th and 10th values:
$$Q_3 = \frac{55 + 60}{2} = 57.5\text{ metres}$$

Step 5: Calculate the Interquartile Range:
$$\mathrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 57.5 - 40 = 17.5\text{ metres}$$

hints: Notice the single extreme value $110$ compared to all other estimates which lie between $30$ and $62$.
Explain how the arithmetic mean is sensitive to extreme values or outliers, unlike the median.
walkthrough:
Identify the effect of the extreme observation on the mean:
$$\text{The dataset contains an extreme outlier } (110\text{ metres}), \text{ which disproportionately affects and inflates the mean.}$$
teacher_walkthrough: We need to state a disadvantage of using the mean as a measure of central tendency for this dataset.

Step 1: Inspect the dataset for anomalies.
Notice that 11 of the 12 tourists gave estimates between $30\text{ m}$ and $62\text{ m}$, while one tourist estimated $110\text{ m}$.

Step 2: Explain the consequence for the mean.
The value $110\text{ m}$ is an extreme outlier. Because the arithmetic mean uses every data value equally in its sum, this single extreme value inflates the mean significantly, making it unrepresentative of the typical tourist estimate.
